name: Capsaicin for hair

card.summary: Capsaicin, the pungent compound in chili peppers, is discussed as a topical or dietary way to support hair growth, via a proposed IGF-1 and sensory-nerve route.
card.note: Capsaicin is a strong skin and eye irritant.

quick.overview:
Capsaicin is the main pungent compound in chili peppers. In hair-growth discussion it is mentioned as a topical or dietary ingredient that might support hair growth through sensory nerves and IGF-1, a growth signal in the hair follicle.

The idea circulates mostly through forum posts and blogs that cite laboratory and early human findings on related compounds; medical use of capsaicin is established for pain relief, not hair.
quick.how: Forum users have discussed capsaicin-containing topicals and supplements, sometimes alongside raspberry ketone or soy isoflavones. Product forms and routines vary and no standard protocol exists.
quick.risks: Capsaicin is a strong irritant to skin, eyes and the lungs and can sensitise tissue; ingestion can cause nausea and burning discomfort, and cardiac events have been reported after capsaicin pills [1].

lead: Capsaicin is the main pungent compound in chili peppers, concentrated in the placental tissue that holds the seeds [1]. It binds the TRPV1 receptor on pain-sensing nerve fibres, and repeated activation can desensitise them, which is why it is used as a topical analgesic [1].

In hair-loss discussion, capsaicin appears as a possible follicle-supporting ingredient. A T Nation forum poster summarised a blog article claiming that capsaicin and soy isoflavones increase IGF-1 and hair growth [2], and another poster linked a paper on raspberry ketone, noting that sensory neurons release the peptide CGRP when activated [3]. This is the proposed mechanism people cite: sensory-nerve activation, CGRP, then IGF-1 in the follicle.
The forum material is the source of the hair claim here; the encyclopedic record covers capsaicin's pain uses and safety and does not mention hair [1].

angle.text: People who use it hope for thicker hair by stimulating the follicle's local growth signalling. The route is proposed from laboratory findings and forum summaries.

paras: Discussion on T Nation links capsaicin to IGF-1 and hair growth, citing a blog summary [2], and mentions heat-based topical products in the context of balding [3]. Another thread collects hair-loss approaches in a single guide article [4].

A capsaicin patch was approved in 2009 by the FDA and EU for post-herpetic neuralgia [1]. A 2017 review found moderate to substantial relief from high-dose topical capsaicin in several neuropathies, with limited evidence quality [1].

Capsaicin binds TRPV1 on nociceptor fibres, depolarising the neuron; repeated activation causes local desensitisation [1]. It reaches the stratum corneum within about a minute of topical application [1].

Capsaicin strongly irritates skin, eyes and lungs and can sensitise tissue [1]. Ingestion can cause nausea, vomiting and burning diarrhoea, and cardiac events have occurred in healthy young people taking capsaicin pills [1].
Related laboratory work on sensory-nerve signalling is cited in forum posts [3], but it concerns a different compound.

lore.intro: Capsaicin for hair appears in T Nation threads on baldness and IGF-1 [2][3][4].

claims.claim: Capsaicin raises IGF-1 and grows hair
claims.believers: A poster cites a blog article saying capsaicin and soy isoflavones increase IGF-1 and hair growth [2].
claims.experts: The standard reference on capsaicin describes pain and irritant effects and does not report hair effects [1].

claims.claim: Sensory-nerve activation via CGRP supports hair growth
claims.believers: Another poster links a paper on topical raspberry ketone and notes that sensory neurons release CGRP on activation [3].
claims.experts: The paper cited concerns raspberry ketone, not capsaicin as a hair treatment.
